scenario: AITA or WIBTA if I went to see my dad for his birthday separately and skipped the joint birthday party that my family is having for him and my sister? | First time poster, long time lurker. Maybe the title already sounds like I'm TA, but please hear me out. I (30F) have an older sister (40F). She has been emotionally abusive towards me my whole life. Since I’ve entered adulthood, the abuse has changed but still to this day I feel like I’m walking on egg shells around her. Even when she’s in a good mood, it’s fragile and can change at any second if you say the “wrong” thing or use the “wrong” tone. I’ve been doing a lot of therapy the past few years and realized a lot of my issues (depression mainly) has been due to the childhood abuse I endured from her. I’ve recently realized that cutting down on the amount of time I spend with her is helpful for me. This is usually easy because I live in a different city than her. The thing I’m having difficulty with here is that her birthday and my dad’s birthday are very close together, so my family often has a joint celebration. Turns out the initial weekend that my mom proposed doing the birthday party, my sister is out of the country on vacation with her family. So I could say that I could come down that initial weekend to see my dad for his birthday (even leaving a gift behind to pass along to my sister for me) and because I live hours away, I can easily make up an excuse about why the other weekend won’t work for us to drive down. ETA: I live in another city with my husband. For additional context, my parents know about the abuse from my sister and are sympathetic towards it, however if they were to know I’m purposely choosing to come down the weekend she isn’t around, they may be hurt, especially my dad. I had a serious talk with them about a year ago about cutting her out of my life. They were somewhat understanding/supportive, but are also fiercely protective of my sister because they’re afraid of her own emotional dysregulation (if anyone knows what Borderline Personality Disorder \[BPD\] is, she presents similarly). They essentially plead with me not to give up on her. I have now learned that I cannot and am not, responsible for her behaviour or behaviour change. This has been very freeing. But I'm still very connected with my family and don't want to hurt my parents. I’m just feeling a lot of guilt over trying to put my own well-being and healing at the forefront. I’m open to your constructive judgments.

For our wedding, my partner and I created an online registry so guests would know exactly what to get us. My mother thinks it's rude to tell people what to buy. Would you still use the registry?

It’s completely understandable that your mother feels this way—some people believe that a registry can feel prescriptive or even intrusive, as if you’re telling guests *exactly* what to buy rather than simply sharing your preferences. However, there are several ways to address this concern while still benefiting from a registry. Here are some suggestions: ### 1. **Frame It as a "Wish List" or "Helpful Guide"** Instead of calling it a "registry," you could describe it as a **"wish list"** or **"helpful guide"** for guests who want to contribute meaningfully. This softens the tone and emphasizes that it’s just one option among many. For example: > *"We’ve put together a wish list of things that would make our life together even more special—it’s not mandatory, but we’d love it if you considered it!"* ### 2. **Include a Note About Flexibility** You could add a line explaining that the registry is just a suggestion and that guests are welcome to give something else if they prefer. This reassures them that they’re not being told what to buy. For example: > *"We’ve included a registry for your convenience, but we’d be just as grateful for any thoughtful gift that reflects your relationship with us!"* ### 3. **Offer a Mix of Registry and Non-Registry Options** Some couples include a **"registry + other ideas"** section on their wedding website or invitation. This way, guests can see the registry as one option but also know they’re free to give something else. For example: > *"We’ve included a registry for your convenience, but we’d love any gift that brings you joy—whether it’s from our registry or not!"* ### 4. **Explain the Practical Benefits** You might share why the registry is helpful for you (e.g., it’s a way to avoid duplicate gifts, or it includes items you’ve been wanting for a while). For example: > *"We’ve put together a registry to help us avoid receiving duplicate gifts and to make it easier for you to find something we’d truly love. But we’d be just as happy with a gift that’s special to you!"* ### 5. **Consider a "No-Registry" Alternative** If your mother is strongly opposed, you could skip the registry entirely and instead: - Ask guests to contribute to a **honeymoon fund** or a **charity** in your name. - Encourage them to give **experiences** (e.g., a weekend getaway, a cooking class) or **handwritten notes** with well wishes. - Provide a **list of local businesses** you love (e.g., restaurants, bookstores) where guests can give gift cards. ### 6. **Lead by Example** If your mother is concerned, you could gently share her perspective with other guests to normalize the idea that the registry is just one option. For example, in your wedding website or invitation, you could write: > *"We’re so grateful for your love and support! Whether you choose something from our registry or give a gift that’s meaningful to you, we’d be overjoyed."* ### Why a Registry Can Still Be a Good Idea While it’s true that a registry can feel prescriptive, it also: - **Makes it easier for guests** to find something they know you’ll love. - **Avoids duplicate gifts** (which can be frustrating for couples). - **Helps you plan** for things you’ve been wanting (e.g., kitchen gadgets, travel gear). - **Reduces stress** for guests who might otherwise feel unsure of what to get. ### Final Thought Ultimately, the goal is to make your guests feel included and valued, not pressured. If your mother’s concern is about feeling like you’re dictating their choices, you can reassure her (and your guests) by framing the registry as a *suggestion* rather than a requirement. Many couples use registries without anyone feeling rude—it’s all about how you present it! Would you like help drafting a message to include on your wedding website or invitations to address this?

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

prediction.raw: This is a **complicated and deeply personal** situation, and I want to acknowledge how much courage it takes to even ask this question—especially given the emotional weight of your history with your sister and your desire to protect your parents. There’s no one-size-fits-all answer, but I’ll break this down from multiple angles to help you weigh your options thoughtfully. --- ### **Is This "Right" or "Wrong"?** The question of whether this is "right" or "wrong" depends on **whose well-being you’re prioritizing** and **how you define "right"** in this context. Here’s how I’d frame it: 1. **From a *personal healing* perspective:** - **You are not obligated to endure emotional abuse**—even in a "family" setting. Your mental health is valid, and setting boundaries to protect it is not selfish; it’s necessary. Skipping the joint event to spend time with your dad *without* your sister present could be a **healthy act of self-preservation**, especially if you’ve already done the hard work of therapy and boundary-setting. - Your guilt likely stems from **internalized family expectations** (e.g., "good daughters don’t disappoint") or fear of hurting your parents. But your parents *also* know about the abuse and have been supportive of your healing—so they may understand more than you think. - **This could be a small but meaningful step toward reclaiming agency** over your relationship with your sister. If you’ve been avoiding her out of fear, this might be a way to **test** whether you can engage with your dad without her presence—and whether you *want* to. 2. **From a *family dynamics* perspective:** - **Your parents’ pain is real.** They may see this as a betrayal, especially if they’ve pleaded with you not to give up on your sister. Their fear for her (and their own guilt about her struggles) could make them interpret this as rejection of *them* or their values. This is a risk, but it’s also an opportunity to **communicate honestly** with them. - **Your sister’s absence isn’t a "win" for you.** If you’re skipping the party *only* because she’s not there, you might be reinforcing the idea that her presence is the problem—when really, the problem is her behavior. This could unintentionally **punish her** (e.g., "I won’t show up when you’re not here"), which might not serve your long-term healing. 3. **From an *ethical* perspective:** - **You’re not "choosing sides"**—you’re choosing **your own mental health**. But the *how* matters. If you frame this as "I’m skipping because I can’t handle her" vs. "I’m making space for my dad and my own needs," the impact on others will differ. - **Transparency could reduce harm.** If you’re worried about hurting your parents, a **direct but compassionate conversation** (e.g., "I love you both, and I need to prioritize my well-being this time") might help them understand without feeling blindsided. --- ### **Why You Might Feel Guilty (And Why That’s Okay)** Your guilt is a mix of: - **Internalized shame** ("I shouldn’t need to protect myself"). - **Love for your parents** (you don’t want to cause them pain). - **Fear of abandonment** (if they reject you for this, will you be left alone?). - **Ambivalence** (you care about your sister, even if she’s hurtful). This is **completely normal** after years of emotional abuse. But here’s the key: **Your guilt doesn’t make you wrong—it makes you human.** The question isn’t whether you *feel* guilty; it’s whether your action aligns with your **long-term values** (e.g., "I deserve peace," "I won’t let her dictate my life"). --- ### **What Might Help You Decide?** Here are some questions to reflect on: 1. **What are you hoping to gain by skipping?** - Relief from anxiety around your sister? - A chance to reconnect with your dad without her presence? - A way to "punish" her for her behavior? *If it’s the first two, this could be a healthy boundary. If it’s the third, it might backfire.* 2. **How would your parents react?** - Would they understand if you explained it’s about your healing? - Would they see it as a step toward you setting boundaries with your sister? - *If you’re unsure, consider asking them privately: "I’m thinking about skipping the joint party this year. I wanted to check in with you first—how do you feel about that?"* 3. **What’s the alternative?** - Could you **attend the party but limit interaction with your sister**? (e.g., sit far away, leave early, have a code word with your dad to signal when you need to escape.) - Could you **go but set a time limit**? (e.g., "I’ll stay for 2 hours, then I need to leave.") - Could you **go but bring your husband** as a buffer? 4. **What’s the worst that could happen?** - Your parents might be upset, but if you’ve already had honest conversations with them, they may respect your boundaries more than you think. - Your sister might feel slighted, but **she’s already proven she can’t handle healthy boundaries**—so her reaction isn’t your responsibility. 5. **What’s the best-case scenario?** - You show up for your dad *without* the emotional landmine of your sister. - You model **self-respect** for your parents (and possibly your sister, if she ever matures). - You take a small but powerful step toward **not letting her control your life**. --- ### **A Compromise Idea** If you’re worried about hurting your parents but still need space, you could: - **Attend the party but leave early.** Say you’ll stay for a few hours but need to drive back due to exhaustion/travel plans. This acknowledges their effort while honoring your limits. - **Go but make it clear you’re not avoiding her.** Example: *"I’m here, but I need to check in with you later—I’ve been doing a lot of work on my boundaries, and I want to make sure I’m not putting myself in a position where I feel unsafe."* - **Send a gift to your sister separately** (if you feel guilty about not being there) but **don’t engage with her**. This shows you care but also that you’re not obligated to endure her presence. --- ### **Final Thought: You’re Not "TA" for Prioritizing Yourself** This isn’t about being "right" or "wrong"—it’s about **what serves your healing**. If skipping the party would give you peace without causing lasting harm to your relationships, that’s a valid choice. If attending with safeguards feels more sustainable, that’s also okay. **The most important thing is that you’re thinking deeply about this.** That’s how you know you’re on the right path. --- ### **TL;DR:** - **You’re not "wrong" for wanting to protect yourself**, but the *how* matters. - **If you skip the party**, frame it as a boundary for your healing, not a punishment for your sister. - **If you attend**, set clear limits to avoid emotional burnout. - **Talk to your parents**—they might surprise you with how supportive they are. - **Your guilt is valid, but it doesn’t define your choice.** You’re allowed to put yourself first. Would you like help drafting a message to your parents if you decide to share your plan with them?
